subject.title: The Dead Man Walking
subject.author: Thomas Hardy
subject.text:
They hail me as one living,
But don't they know
That I have died of late years,
Untombed although?

I am but a shape that stands here,
A pulseless mould,
A pale past picture, screening
Ashes gone cold.

Not at a minute's warning,
Not in a loud hour,
For me ceased Time's enchantments
In hall and bower.

There was no tragic transit,
No catch of breath,
When silent seasons inched me
On to this death ....

- A Troubadour-youth I rambled
With Life for lyre,
The beats of being raging
In me like fire.

But when I practised eyeing
The goal of men,
It iced me, and I perished
A little then.

When passed my friend, my kinsfolk,
Through the Last Door,
And left me standing bleakly,
I died yet more;

And when my Love's heart kindled
In hate of me,
Wherefore I knew not, died I
One more degree.

And if when I died fully
I cannot say,
And changed into the corpse-thing
I am to-day,

Yet is it that, though whiling
The time somehow
In walking, talking, smiling,
I live not now.

title: The Date Hardy Left Off the Page
standfirst: In Time's Laughingstocks (1909), Thomas Hardy dated poem after poem to a specific year — 1867, 1897, 1904. The one about a man who cannot say exactly when he died, he left with no date at all.

sections.heading: Ten Stanzas, Long Line Then Short
sections.body:
Hardy builds "The Dead Man Walking" out of ten four-line stanzas, and nearly every one runs the same small trick: a longer, unrhymed line, then a short one that rhymes, twice over.

> They hail me as one living,
> But don't they know
> That I have died of late years,
> Untombed although?

The long lines carry the sentence; the short ones land the blow. For nine stanzas running, only those short lines rhyme with each other — *know* against *although*, *hour* against *bower*, *breath* against *death* — while the long ones never answer anything. It is only in the very last stanza that all four lines finally lock together:

> Yet is it that, though whiling
> The time somehow
> In walking, talking, smiling,
> I live not now.

*Whiling* answers *smiling* there, not just *somehow* answering *now*. The one stanza where the form stops interrupting itself is the one where the speaker finally declares himself, completely, dead.

sections.heading: The Year Missing From the Page
sections.body:
*Time's Laughingstocks and Other Verses*, the 1909 collection this poem belongs to, is full of poems Hardy dated precisely — a year printed directly beneath the text, the way he did throughout his career as a poet. Reading through [the 1909 first edition itself](https://archive.org/details/timeslaughingsto00harduoft), dates turn up again and again in that same book: 1867, 1871, 1883, 1897, twice in 1901, 1902, 1904, 1906. "The Dead Man Walking" carries none of them. It runs straight from its final stanza into the next poem's title with nothing printed in between.

That has not stopped later summaries from assigning it one anyway; several put the poem's composition around 1890, roughly two decades before it reached print. None of them cite a letter, a manuscript or anything else in Hardy's own hand to support that figure, and it appears nowhere in the book. Nothing here firms the date up, so the honest answer is that nobody, on the evidence available, actually knows when Hardy wrote it.

sections.heading: The Alibi Hardy Built In
sections.body:
Hardy insisted, of poems like this one, that behind their "I" stood not autobiography but ["dramatic monologues by different characters"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time%27s_Laughingstocks_and_Other_Verses) — a defence he offered often enough that it reads as pre-emptive as much as theoretical. He made the same claim about the book's own title, which he called, in his words, a poetic image only, and not to be taken as a philosophical belief.

The poem does not make the defence easy. Its stages track, in order, the stages of a specific kind of life: a young man with literary ambition (*A Troubadour-youth I rambled / With Life for lyre*), that ambition curdling on contact with worldly judgment, the deaths of friends and family thinning out around him, and a marriage that soured into something the speaker can only call hatred. None of that proves anything — a monologue can borrow the shape of a life without confessing to it — but it is a specific shape to have invented from nothing.

sections.heading: A House Designed by the Man Who Grew Estranged In It
sections.body:
Hardy married Emma Gifford on 17 September 1874, and in 1885 the couple moved into Max Gate, the house outside Dorchester that [Hardy had designed himself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy). It was where they lived out the following decades of a marriage that, by the standard account of his life, became estranged well before Emma's death in 1912. One specific wound is documented: Emma worried that *Jude the Obscure*, published in 1895, carried the marks of their own marriage's unhappiness onto the page for anyone to read.

Whether "The Dead Man Walking" is about that marriage or, as Hardy's account of his own poems would have it, no marriage in particular, the line that names the wound is unambiguous even if its target is not: *And when my Love's heart kindled / In hate of me, / Wherefore I knew not, died I / One more degree.* *Wherefore I knew not* — the speaker's own bewilderment at the cause is, whatever its source, exactly the kind of thing a poet protects himself by calling a monologue.

sections.heading: The Novelist Who Said He Never Much Cared
sections.body:
*Jude the Obscure* was Hardy's last novel. Its reception was harsh enough that later readers have assumed the backlash drove him out of fiction; Hardy's own explanation was blunter, and he insisted it had nothing to do with the reviews — he said he had [never cared very much about writing novels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy) and felt he had written quite enough of them. Either way, *Wessex Poems*, his first collection, followed in 1898, three years after his last novel and eleven years before *Time's Laughingstocks*.

*But when I practised eyeing / The goal of men, / It iced me, and I perished / A little then* reads, against that career, like a description of the exact moment ambition stopped being warm. Nothing pins those four lines to 1895 specifically — the poem carries no date, and Hardy gave the moment it describes no name at all — but a writer who had just spent a quarter-century meeting the goal of men on its own terms, novel after novel, had earned the right to say what that felt like once it was over.

sections.heading: The Grief That Revised the Story
sections.body:
Emma Gifford died in November 1912. What followed was [Poems of 1912–13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poems_1912%E2%80%9313), the elegy sequence built out of Hardy's grief and a pilgrimage back to the Cornwall coast where the couple had first met, decades before Max Gate and everything that came after. Set beside *Time's Laughingstocks*, the sequence reads close to a retraction: where "The Dead Man Walking" gives a marriage one flat, bewildered line about hatred, *Poems of 1912–13* spends more than twenty poems trying to recover what Hardy's own biography describes as those places and the happier times that had gone with them.

Fourteen months separate a wife's death from a book of poems that changed how her husband wrote about loving her. No comparable record exists for whatever changed, or didn't, between whenever "The Dead Man Walking" was actually written and whenever it reached print in 1909. The poem's own speaker cannot say exactly when he died. The book that holds it will not say exactly when it was written, either.
